summary.text: The singular value decomposition factors a real or complex matrix into a rotation, followed by a scaling, followed by another rotation.
It generalizes the eigendecomposition of a square normal matrix to any m × n matrix, and such a decomposition always exists.
Its singular values give the size of the stretching, and it is used for pseudoinverses, matrix approximation, signal processing and least squares fitting.

facts.label: Singular values
facts.value: The scaling entries, usually listed from largest to smallest

facts.label: Rank link
facts.value: The number of non-zero singular values equals the matrix's rank

facts.label: Ellipse picture
facts.value: In 2D, singular values are the semiaxes of an ellipse

facts.label: Size and direction
facts.value: Singular values encode magnitude; singular vectors encode direction

facts.label: Uniqueness
facts.value: The decomposition itself is not unique in general

items.prompt: Into which three geometric steps does the decomposition break any linear transformation of ordinary space?

options.label: A shear, then a shift, then a further rotation
A rotation, a scaling, then another rotation
Three scalings along three separate axes
A rotation, then a projection, then a shear

items.explain: The factors are a rotation or reflection, a coordinate-by-coordinate scaling, and another rotation or reflection.

items.prompt: A matrix has exactly two non-zero singular values and all its other singular values are zero. What is its rank?

options.label: Zero
Two
Equal to its number of rows
Impossible to tell

items.explain: The number of non-zero singular values, repetitions included, equals the rank.

items.prompt: A picture of a 2D transformation shows an ellipse. What do the singular values correspond to?

options.label: The directions the ellipse is tilted toward
The area enclosed by the ellipse
The number of corners of the shape
The lengths of the ellipse's semiaxes

items.explain: Singular values can be read as the magnitudes of the semiaxes of an ellipse in 2D.

items.prompt: You want to know in which direction a matrix stretches things, not by how much. What should you look at?

options.label: The singular vectors
The singular values
The rank
The largest entry

items.explain: Singular vectors encode direction, while singular values encode magnitude.

items.prompt: A matrix is not square, say with more columns than rows. Does it still have such a decomposition?

options.label: No, only square matrices have one
Yes, but only when its entries are real
Yes, any real or complex matrix has one
No, it needs a positive determinant

items.explain: It generalizes the eigendecomposition to any m × n matrix, and the decomposition always exists for a complex matrix.

items.prompt: Ignoring order, two people each compute the decomposition of the same matrix. What must agree between them?

options.label: Every factor matrix, entry by entry
Nothing, the results are arbitrary
Only the left factor
The singular values, though the factors may differ

items.explain: The singular values are uniquely determined up to reordering, but the decomposition in general is not unique.

paragraphs.heading: Three simple moves
paragraphs.text: The singular value decomposition, or SVD, breaks a real or complex matrix into three steps: a rotation, then a scaling, then another rotation. It extends the eigendecomposition, which needs a square normal matrix with an orthonormal eigenbasis, so that it works for any m × n matrix. Such a decomposition exists for every complex matrix.

paragraphs.heading: The pieces
paragraphs.text: Written out, the SVD of an m × n complex matrix M is 𝐌 = 𝐔𝜮𝐕^(∗). Here U is an m × m unitary matrix and V is an n × n unitary matrix, while V^(∗) stands for the conjugate transpose of V. The middle factor 𝜮 is a rectangular m × n diagonal matrix whose diagonal holds real numbers that are never negative. Those numbers are the singular values of M; M fixes them up to their order, and they are usually listed from largest to smallest. The columns of U are called left-singular vectors and the columns of V right-singular vectors.

paragraphs.heading: Seeing it in space
paragraphs.text: For a real square matrix, think of M as a transformation of space. The SVD splits it into a rotation or reflection, then a scaling of each coordinate by its singular value, then another rotation or reflection. Another picture: M carries the unit sphere onto an ellipsoid, and the non-zero singular values are the lengths of that ellipsoid's semi-axes. The singular values give the sizes of those axes, and the singular vectors give their directions.

paragraphs.heading: Rank and building blocks
paragraphs.text: The count of non-zero singular values, repeats included, equals the rank r of M. With the singular values sorted, the SVD writes M as r rank-1 matrices added together, one for each singular value. The first r columns of U give a basis for the column space of M. The last n − r columns of V give a basis for its null space.

paragraphs.heading: What it is used for
paragraphs.text: In mathematics, the SVD is used to compute the pseudoinverse, to approximate matrices, and to find a matrix's rank, range and null space. It is a common way to carry out low-rank approximation. Science, engineering and statistics rely on it too, for jobs like signal processing, process control and least squares fitting of data.

paragraphs.heading: Rotations, reflections and signs
paragraphs.text: For a real square matrix, the sign of the determinant says something about the outer factors. If the determinant is positive, U and V^(∗) can both be chosen as rotations with reflections, or both as rotations without. If it is negative, exactly one of them has a reflection. If it is zero, each can be picked as either type on its own.

paragraphs.heading: Compared with eigenvectors
paragraphs.text: If M happens to be Hermitian and positive-semidefinite, U and V are both the same unitary matrix that diagonalizes M. When M is diagonalizable but not of that kind, its eigendecomposition and its SVD differ.
